objectives: Trace toxicology from Paracelsus + Orfila + Marsh through Casarett-Doull + Klaassen + WHO + ECHA.
Classify xenobiotics by source + duration + reversibility.
Distinguish endogenous vs exogenous + acute vs chronic + reversible vs irreversible exposures.

slides.title: The founders: Paracelsus, Orfila, Marsh + the birth of a science
slides.body:
**Toxicology** is the science of poisons + adverse effects of chemicals on living organisms. Distinct from pharmacology (therapeutic actions) + epidemiology (population disease distribution) + public health (organized prevention) — toxicology asks: *what does a chemical do, at what dose, to which target?*

**Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, 1493-1541)** — Swiss-German physician + alchemist. His Drei Bücher der Wundartzney (1538) + Septem Defensiones famously asserted **'Sola dosis facit venenum'** — 'the dose alone makes the poison.' A revolutionary reframing: *every* substance is potentially toxic; only the dose distinguishes a medicine from a poison. Set the foundation for the dose-response principle that defines all of toxicology. He rejected Galenic humoral medicine + championed minerals + chemical preparations (mercury, arsenic, antimony) — both pioneering pharmaceutical chemistry + foreshadowing iatrogenic poisoning.

**Mathieu Joseph Bonaventure Orfila (1787-1853)** — Spanish-French physician, dean of the Paris medical faculty. His **Traité des poisons** (Treatise on Poisons, 1813-1815) is the founding text of forensic + analytical toxicology. Orfila systematically catalogued poisons by source (mineral, vegetable, animal), described their physiological effects in animal experiments + human cases, + developed chemical detection methods. Acted as expert witness in the celebrated **Marie LaFarge arsenic poisoning trial (1840)** — establishing forensic toxicology as a courtroom discipline. The 'father of toxicology.'

**James Marsh (1794-1846)** — English chemist at the Royal Arsenic Test. Developed the **Marsh test (1836)** for arsenic: zinc + sulfuric acid + arsenic-containing sample → arsine gas (AsH₃) → heated → deposits metallic arsenic 'mirror' on cooled surface. Sensitive to 0.02 mg + reproducible — finally making arsenic detection reliable in postmortem tissues. Solved the long-standing 'inheritance powder' problem (acute arsenic poisoning was a frequent murder method). Used dramatically in the LaFarge trial by Orfila. Modern atomic absorption + ICP-MS replaced the Marsh test in routine use, but it remains a teaching exemplar.

**François Magendie (1783-1855)** — French physiologist; established systematic animal experimentation in pharmacology + toxicology. Studied strychnine + emetine + opium alkaloids; demonstrated reproducible dose-effect relationships + organ specificity. Founded the Journal de Physiologie (1821). His pupil **Claude Bernard (1813-1878)** — author of An Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine (1865), the methodological canon of biomedical science — applied physiology to toxicology: showed that curare blocked neuromuscular transmission (without affecting nerve or muscle directly) + that carbon monoxide bound hemoglobin (displacing O₂). Bernard's milieu intérieur concept + the principle that **the same substance affects different organs through different mechanisms** founded mechanistic toxicology.

**Theodore Wormley (1826-1897)** — American chemist + physician; his **Micro-Chemistry of Poisons** (1867, expanded 1885) was the standard American forensic-toxicology reference for half a century. Detailed microcrystalline + color-reaction tests for alkaloids + metals; bridged Orfila's continental tradition to US courtrooms + medical schools.

Together these founders established: (1) the dose-response principle (Paracelsus); (2) systematic classification + forensic application (Orfila); (3) reliable analytical detection (Marsh); (4) experimental physiology + organ-specific mechanisms (Magendie + Bernard); (5) the courtroom-laboratory-textbook integration (Wormley).

slides.title: Modern toxicology: Sax, Casarett-Doull, Klaassen, WHO, ECHA, EPA
slides.body:
**N. Irving Sax (1903-1988)** — author of **Dangerous Properties of Industrial Materials** (Sax 1957+; now Lewis-Sax in successive editions). The encyclopedic reference for industrial chemicals: physical-chemical properties, toxicity data, exposure limits, regulatory status. ~30000 substances catalogued in current editions. Indispensable in industrial hygiene + occupational toxicology.

**Casarett + Doull's Toxicology: The Basic Science of Poisons** — first edition Louis Casarett + John Doull 1975; **Curtis D. Klaassen** assumed editorship 1980+; now in its 10th edition (Klaassen 2024). The canonical academic textbook of toxicology — every modern toxicologist trains on it. Organizes the field into: general principles (dose-response, kinetics, mechanisms), disposition (absorption + distribution + metabolism + excretion), non-organ-directed toxicity (genetic, developmental, carcinogenesis), organ-specific toxicology, toxic agents (metals, solvents, pesticides), environmental toxicology, applications (regulatory, clinical, forensic). The 'Casarett-Doull' or 'Klaassen' framework structures graduate curricula + board exams.

**Edward J. Calabrese** — University of Massachusetts toxicologist; reframed dose-response with **hormesis** (covered in dose-response lesson): biphasic curves where low-dose stimulation accompanies high-dose inhibition. Maintains BELLE (Biological Effects of Low Level Exposures) + has driven regulatory reconsideration of low-dose linearity assumptions.

**Theodore A. Loomis** — co-author of Essentials of Toxicology (Loomis-Hayes); popularized the term **xenobiotic** (xeno = foreign + bios = life) for substances foreign to a biological system. Modern usage: any chemical not normally present in or expected to be in an organism — drugs, pollutants, food additives, industrial chemicals, pesticides, cosmetics. Distinct from **endogenous** substances (hormones, neurotransmitters, metabolites) — though endogenous compounds can be toxic at supraphysiological doses (Paracelsus revisited).

**International + regulatory toxicology**:
- **WHO + the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA)** + JMPR (Joint Meeting on Pesticide Residues): set Acceptable Daily Intakes (ADIs) + Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs).
- **IPCS (International Programme on Chemical Safety)** — WHO + ILO + UNEP joint programme; produces Environmental Health Criteria (EHC) + Concise International Chemical Assessment Documents (CICADs); harmonizes risk-assessment terminology.
- **ECHA (European Chemicals Agency, Helsinki, 2007)** administers **REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation, and Restriction of Chemicals, EC 1907/2006)** — landmark EU regulation requiring registration + safety assessment of ~30000+ chemicals; 'no data, no market.'
- **EPA + TSCA (Toxic Substances Control Act 1976; Frank R. Lautenberg Chemical Safety Act amendments 2016)** — US equivalent; covers industrial chemicals (cosmetics + pesticides separately regulated under FFDCA + FIFRA).
- **ATSDR (Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, 1980)** — CDC sister agency; produces Toxicological Profiles for Superfund chemicals + the ATSDR Substance Priority List (lead + arsenic + mercury + vinyl chloride + PCBs + benzene perennially top-ranked).
- **IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer, Lyon, 1965)** — WHO body; classifies carcinogens into Group 1 (known), 2A (probable), 2B (possible), 3 (not classifiable), 4 (probably not — single agent caprolactam).

These institutional structures convert toxicological science into regulatory action — defining the chemical safety landscape of the modern world.

slides.title: Classification: xenobiotics, exposure type, duration, reversibility
slides.body:
**Xenobiotic** (Loomis) — a chemical foreign to a biological system. Categories by source:
- **Drugs + pharmaceuticals**: therapeutic intent; toxicity emerges at supra-therapeutic doses or in idiosyncratic individuals (e.g., acetaminophen NAPQI in overdose).
- **Environmental pollutants**: lead, mercury, dioxins, PCBs, PFAS, pesticides, industrial solvents.
- **Natural toxins**: ricin (Ricinus communis), tetrodotoxin (Tetraodontidae), botulinum toxin, snake + scorpion + spider venoms, mycotoxins (aflatoxin), microcystins.
- **Food additives + contaminants**: preservatives, colorants, pesticide residues, packaging migrants (BPA, phthalates), processing contaminants (acrylamide, heterocyclic amines).
- **Recreational drugs + drugs of abuse**: alcohol, opioids, stimulants, hallucinogens.
- **Cosmetics + personal care**: phthalates, parabens, formaldehyde, UV filters.
- **Occupational chemicals**: silica, asbestos, benzene, solvents.

**Endogenous vs exogenous**:
- **Exogenous** = xenobiotic (entered from outside).
- **Endogenous** = produced by the organism (hormones, neurotransmitters, intermediary metabolites). Can become toxic at supraphysiological levels — e.g., bilirubin (kernicterus), uric acid (gout), phenylalanine (PKU), iron (hemochromatosis), copper (Wilson disease), vitamins A + D + E + K (hypervitaminoses).

**Exposure duration** (NTP + IPCS conventions):
- **Acute**: single exposure or multiple within ~24 h. Examples: cyanide ingestion, snake bite, carbon-monoxide poisoning, single-dose drug overdose.
- **Subacute (subchronic)**: ~14 days to 90 days repeated exposure. Examples: subchronic feeding studies in regulatory toxicology.
- **Chronic**: >3 months (or >10% of lifespan in lab animals). Examples: occupational lead, asbestos, chronic alcohol, environmental PFAS, long-term medications.

**Reversible vs irreversible effects**:
- **Reversible**: effect resolves after exposure ceases. E.g., reversible cholinesterase inhibition by carbamates; CNS depression from ethanol; histamine release from a single dose.
- **Irreversible**: persistent damage even after exposure stops. E.g., aplastic anemia from benzene; mesothelioma decades after asbestos; cirrhosis from chronic alcohol; aristolochic-acid nephropathy; neurodegeneration from MPTP-induced parkinsonism (Langston); some teratogenic effects (thalidomide phocomelia); somatic mutations leading to cancer.

**Local vs systemic**:
- **Local**: at the site of contact (skin corrosion, eye injury, respiratory irritation, GI corrosion).
- **Systemic**: requires absorption + distribution to target organ (lead encephalopathy after gut absorption; methanol blindness after hepatic conversion to formate).

**Idiosyncratic vs predictable**:
- **Predictable (type A; augmented)**: dose-related, mechanistically understood, affecting most exposed individuals.
- **Idiosyncratic (type B; bizarre)**: unpredictable, often immune-mediated or pharmacogenetic, affecting rare individuals (e.g., abacavir HLA-B*57:01 hypersensitivity; halothane hepatitis; succinylcholine apnea in pseudocholinesterase deficiency).

**Allergic + hypersensitivity reactions**: immune-mediated; require prior sensitization; not strictly dose-dependent (very low re-exposure can trigger severe response). Type I (IgE; anaphylaxis), Type II (cytotoxic), Type III (immune-complex), Type IV (T-cell delayed).

These classifications structure: study design (acute LD50 vs chronic bioassay), regulation (different test batteries), clinical evaluation (timing of onset distinguishes idiosyncratic from predictable), + risk communication (reversibility shapes how patients + populations weigh exposures).

question.question: Classify three real-world exposures across the toxicology framework
question.goal: For each scenario, classify by: (i) xenobiotic vs endogenous, (ii) exposure duration (acute/subacute/chronic), (iii) reversibility, (iv) local vs systemic, (v) predictable vs idiosyncratic. (A) A 22-year-old ingests 20 g acetaminophen in a suicide attempt. (B) An asbestos shipyard worker (1955-1975) presents in 2020 with mesothelioma. (C) A patient develops Stevens-Johnson syndrome after one week of carbamazepine.

acceptedAnswers: xenobiotic, acute, partly reversible if early NAC, systemic, predictable

steps.reveal: Acetaminophen overdose: (i) xenobiotic (pharmaceutical); (ii) acute (single ingestion); (iii) potentially reversible if N-acetylcysteine given within ~8-10 h (replenishes glutathione + neutralizes NAPQI) — irreversible hepatic necrosis + potential transplant or death if delayed; (iv) systemic (liver target organ — Phase I CYP2E1 + CYP3A4 produces NAPQI when glutathione depleted); (v) predictable + dose-related — covered by Rumack-Matthew nomogram (forensic + clinical lesson).

acceptedAnswers: xenobiotic, chronic, irreversible, local then systemic, predictable in exposed population

steps.reveal: Asbestos mesothelioma: (i) xenobiotic (natural mineral fiber); (ii) chronic occupational (decades); (iii) irreversible (transformation to malignancy is permanent + uniformly fatal historically); (iv) local at lung pleura then potentially systemic metastasis; (v) population-level predictable from dose-response established by Irving Selikoff (Mount Sinai 1964-1979) + IARC Group 1 — but individual susceptibility varies. Latency 30-50 yr (Selikoff's shipyard cohorts). Covered in occupational-toxicology lesson.

acceptedAnswers: xenobiotic, subacute, partly reversible, systemic, idiosyncratic (HLA-B*1502 pharmacogenetic)

steps.reveal: Carbamazepine Stevens-Johnson syndrome: (i) xenobiotic (anticonvulsant); (ii) subacute onset within 1-8 wk of starting; (iii) partially reversible (skin re-epithelializes; mortality 5-15%; long-term sequelae include ocular scarring); (iv) systemic (skin + mucosa + sometimes organs); (v) idiosyncratic + pharmacogenetic — HLA-B*1502 (Han Chinese + Thai + Filipino populations) is strongly associated (Chung 2004; OR > 1000). FDA labeling recommends HLA testing before starting in at-risk populations. Demonstrates how genotype-environment interaction makes some 'idiosyncratic' reactions actually predictable + screenable.

steps.prompt: Why does the classification matter clinically + for regulation?

acceptedAnswers: drives study design + clinical decisions + regulatory action

steps.reveal: Classification drives: (1) **study design** — acute LD50 vs subchronic 90-day vs chronic 2-year bioassay (NTP framework); (2) **clinical decisions** — acute = antidote + supportive; chronic = removal from exposure + long-term surveillance; (3) **regulatory action** — REACH classification thresholds; OSHA PEL setting via TLV-TWA vs acute STEL; (4) **risk communication** — irreversibility (cancer, neurodegeneration) shapes how populations weigh exposures vs reversible (cholinergic excess from carbamates). Casarett-Doull + ECHA + EPA all organize their reference frameworks around these categories.

question.question: Why is Paracelsus's dictum 'sola dosis facit venenum' the foundational principle of toxicology?
options: Because some chemicals are intrinsically safe at any dose.

Because it asserts that every substance can be toxic + that dose alone (not classification as 'natural' or 'synthetic') determines toxicity — establishing the dose-response relationship as the unifying axiom + rejecting essentialist views of poison.
Because it identifies a specific class of poisons.
question.explanation: Paracelsus (1538) — 'sola dosis facit venenum' / 'the dose alone makes the poison.' Foundational because it (i) asserts every substance is potentially toxic at sufficient dose, including water (hyponatremia from acute overload) + oxygen (hyperoxia) + glucose (hyperglycemia); (ii) rejects essentialist categories (the natural vs synthetic distinction does not determine safety — botulinum + ricin + aflatoxin are natural; aspirin + saline are synthetic + low-toxicity); (iii) establishes the **dose-response** as the central quantitative concept (covered in lesson 2); (iv) frames every toxicology question as 'at what dose, in whom, by what route, over what duration?' Modern reframings: hormesis (Calabrese), endocrine disruption (Vandenberg low-dose, non-monotonic), idiosyncratic + pharmacogenetic reactions — but Paracelsus's principle remains the conceptual core. The dose-response curve in lesson 2 operationalizes it.

hints: What does the quote actually say?
slides.workedSolution: Paracelsus (1538) — every substance is potentially toxic; dose alone distinguishes medicine from poison. Foundational because it rejects categorical (natural/synthetic) views + frames toxicology as quantitative dose-response. Universal: water + oxygen + glucose can kill at extreme doses; botulinum + ricin are natural; saline is synthetic + safe. Operationalized by the dose-response curve (lesson 2).

question.question: Building a toxicological evaluation programme for a new industrial chemical
question.prompt: You are a toxicologist at a chemical-manufacturing company developing a new industrial solvent expected to be produced at >1000 tons/year. EU REACH + US TSCA both apply. Discuss: (a) the tiered testing strategy you would design (acute oral + dermal + inhalation LD50; skin/eye irritation; sensitization; subchronic 90-day; chronic 2-year + 2-generation reproductive; genotoxicity battery; carcinogenicity); (b) which Casarett-Doull organ systems you must address; (c) how the dossier feeds into REACH registration + ECHA classification (CMR — carcinogenic/mutagenic/reprotoxic — endpoints) + TSCA Section 5 PMN; (d) when in vitro alternatives (Tox21, ToxCast, organ-on-chip — covered in modern-frontier lesson) would substitute for animal studies + the 3Rs (Russell + Burch) principle of reduce/refine/replace; (e) post-market surveillance via biomonitoring + sentinel cohorts + how this connects to IPCS Environmental Health Criteria + ATSDR profiles if listed on the SPL.

question.question: Acetaminophen has an oral LD50 in rats of ~2400 mg/kg + a typical adult therapeutic dose of ~1 g (≈ 15 mg/kg in a 70 kg adult). What is the approximate margin (LD50 / therapeutic dose, both in mg/kg)?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how Paracelsus (1538) + Orfila (1813) + Marsh (1836) + Bernard (1865) + Casarett-Doull + Klaassen + WHO IPCS + ECHA REACH + EPA TSCA together define modern toxicology.
question.rubric: Mentions: Paracelsus (1538) — dose makes the poison + the dose-response foundation; Orfila (1813 Traité des poisons) — first systematic classification + forensic application + LaFarge trial 1840; Marsh (1836) — reliable arsenic test enabling forensic detection; Magendie + Bernard (1865 Introduction to Experimental Medicine) — animal experimentation + mechanistic + organ-specific toxicology (curare, CO); Wormley — American micro-chemical analysis; Casarett-Doull (1975+) + Klaassen — the canonical academic text structuring the modern field; WHO + IPCS + JECFA + ECHA REACH + EPA TSCA + ATSDR + IARC — the regulatory + risk-assessment infrastructure converting toxicology into chemical safety policy. Concludes: modern toxicology = quantitative dose-response (Paracelsus) + mechanistic organ-specific (Bernard + Casarett-Doull) + forensic-analytical (Orfila + Marsh + Wormley) + regulatory-institutional (WHO + ECHA + EPA).
